detail.abstract: This paper explores the significance and scope of moral rights under the Indian Copyright Act, 1957, emphasizing Section 57 which embodies the author's right to claim authorship and to protect the integrity of their work. Unlike economic rights, moral rights safeguard the author's personality and reputation embedded in the creative expression. The study examines the philosophical foundation of these rights, their recognition in Indian jurisprudence, and comparative insights from international conventions such as the Berne Convention. The paper particularly analyzes landmark cases including Amarnath Sehgal v. Union of India and subsequent judicial interpretations to understand how Indian courts have upheld authors' moral rights. It concludes by discussing contemporary challenges in enforcing these rights in the digital and AI-driven creative landscape.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a performance analysis of a hydropower scheduling model using scenario-based parallelization in a stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) framework. We present significant advancements in the parallel performance of an SDDP-based algorithm, allowing us to leverage the increased computational power offered by modern high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure. The optimization involved in utilizing these powerful systems includes parallel work partitioning strategy and parallel task distribution. The performance analysis shows a notable reduction in runtime as well as a larger region of number of processes with sustained parallel performance. We demonstrate very good performance and scaling, maintaining a parallel efficiency of over 30% even at processor core counts above 400. The analysis also highlights the scalability of the algorithm on large datasets and suggests its potential for wider applications with improved computational efficiency. This paper provides valuable insights into leveraging HPC resources for accelerating complex algorithms, paving the way for future research and development in this area.

detail.abstract: This study examines how national school feeding programmes institutionalise welfare entitlement across India, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Using a comparative lens, it analyses India's PM POSHAN as an education-linked quasi-universal entitlement, Japan's Gakkō Kyūshoku as a universal dignity-first model, and the UK's Free School Meals (FSM) as a household means-tested safety net. The analysis identifies three distinct legitimacy architectures: Japan's normative universalism anchored at the institutional level; the UK's residual means-testing prioritising fiscal discipline; and India's layered quasi-universalism driven by rights discourse and administrative capacity. The paper proposes the Feeding Policy Entitlement and Justification Framework (FPEF), arguing that school feeding is a "legitimacy-first" instrument where equity and stigma depend on whether entitlement is anchored in the institution or the household. These findings offer critical insights for comparative welfare scholarship and policy design in low-and middle-income countries.

title: Autonomous Algorithmic Collusion: Efficient Learning with Q-Function Approximation

detail.title: Autonomous Algorithmic Collusion: Efficient Learning with Q-Function Approximation
detail.abstract: Autonomous algorithmic collusion occurs when firms delegate to autonomous algorithms that learn to collude with each other through repeated interaction. In this paper, I show how efficient learning algorithms can dramatically increase the speed and perfection of autonomous algorithmic collusion. I consider Q-learning pricing algorithms with a parsimonious Q-function that scales linearly in the dimension of the state representation. This allows the algorithms to condition on a higher dimensional representation of the price history, and to better distinguish between temporary and sustained competitor deviation from collusive prices. The algorithms can coordinate quickly on symmetric joint-profit-maximizing collusive prices in a repeated simultaneous oligopoly pricing game. I explore the robustness of collusive prices to the algorithms' parametrization and the strategic environment, and conclude with implications for competition policy.

title: Randomized Promises in a Moral Hazard Model
affiliations: and Stephen M. Ross School of Business, University of Michigan

detail.title: Randomized Promises in a Moral Hazard Model
detail.abstract: We consider a standard moral hazard model with a risk-neutral principal and a strictly risk-averse agent whose preferences are separable in wealth and effort. We identify conditions in both a single-period and a two-period setting in which stochastic contracts that feature ex ante randomization are optimal. In the single-period setting, they can be optimal when the contract must satisfy an individual rationality constraint for the agent, but not when a limited liability constraint binds. An ex ante individual rationality constraint in a single-period setting acts like a promise-keeping constraint in the two-period model. In the dynamic model, even when the agent has limited liability, the optimal contract may be stochastic. We show that stochastic contracts can be optimal when the agent is strictly risk-averse, but not when the agent is risk-neutral.

title: The Payoff–Source Motivation Model: A Three-Path Architecture of Psychological Rewards
affiliations: The Australian National University

detail.title: The Payoff–Source Motivation Model: A Three-Path Architecture of Psychological Rewards
detail.abstract:
People often perform similar prosocial behaviors but with different psychological rewards. Some individuals rely on direct interpersonal responses, like gratitude or reciprocity; others depend on third-party evaluation, and some derive value internally even when no one observes their behavior. Existing research examines these motives separately, leaving no clear structure that could clearly show when each type of payoff dominates and how they interact. This working paper proposes the Payoff–Source Motivation Model (PSMM), a framework that distinguishes motivational pathways based on the psychological reward sources:
(1) Path 1: direct interpersonal payoff
(2) Path 2: third-party or social payoff
(3) Path 3: self-generated payoff
The model introduces simple but expressive updating rules: 
(1) An inverted-U response to positive payoff across all paths;
(2) A purpose-conditioned negative updating rule for social-facing paths (Path 1 and Path 2), where the effect of negative events depends on baseline importance and currentpurpose;
(3) An identity-based rule governing negative self-generated payoff (Path 3).
All these rules generate a dynamic system with local attractors, dominant-path shifts, and cross-path rebalancing.
The goal of this working paper is not to provide a fully-parameterized model, but to lay out a structural foundation for understanding how people allocate motivational weight across payoff sources. Why do similar actions lead to different psychological experiences? How long-term motivational patterns evolve? This framework defines the conceptual space for future formal modeling, empirical testing, and cross-disciplinary integration.

detail.abstract: The United States of Hunger is a searing political essay that exposes the contradiction at the heart of the American project: a nation that praises freedom while punishing truth, and that celebrates justice while weaponizing hunger against the vulnerable. Through personal testimony and rigorous political reflection, Samuel Martínez Roque examines how systems built to protect the people become tools of coercion for immigrants, where reporting abuse results in retaliation, where police defend threats as "protected speech," and where bureaucracy functions as a modern form of cruelty. This essay exposes hunger as a political instrument, silence as a survival strategy, and truth as an act of rebellion. Loud, and without permission, Martínez Roque reveals how deprivation becomes policy, how the border becomes a stomach that digests the poor, and how liberty becomes a privilege reserved for those whose lives the system values. A philosophical, legal, and deeply human indictment of the American myth, The United States of Hunger asks the question the nation fears most: what kind of freedom is it when your survival depends not on how much English you speak, but on how much truth you can swallow just to be allowed to eat?

title: Contingency or Liquidity: Cash Transactions in Housing Markets
affiliations: Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) - Saunders College of Business and UNC Charlotte

detail.title: Contingency or Liquidity: Cash Transactions in Housing Markets
detail.abstract: We study how lender-backed cash financing (LBCF), a mortgage innovation introduced by local community banks to compete with all-cash offers, reshapes the mortgage–cash premium in post-pandemic housing markets. Using data from three large cities in upstate New York, we show that LBCF transactions command a substantial price premium, are associated with a higher incidence of bidding wars, and induce statedependent wedges across competition regimes. An eligibility-frontier difference-indifferences design provides quasi-experimental evidence that access to cash-like execution is capitalized into prices as buyer to-seller surplus transfers, with affordability implications for ineligible borrowers.

title: Intergenerational Mobility in Welfare: Wages and Amenities
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, Duke University and Duke University

detail.title: Intergenerational Mobility in Welfare: Wages and Amenities
detail.abstract: Measures of intergenerational mobility primarily focus on earnings and often overlook substantial heterogeneity in job amenities. We propose a novel measure of intergenerational welfare mobility, "value-value" slope, including both pecuniary and non-pecuniary value of a job. We apply a revealed preference approach to construct common rankings of jobs based on worker flows. Using Danish administrative data, we document that there is 31% more intergenerational mobility than earnings-based mobility measures alone would suggest: the value-value slope is 0.105 and the wage-premia slope is 0.151. Importantly, this aggregate pattern masks striking gender differences: comparing within each gender, daughters exhibit 38% greater mobility in total welfare than in wages; for sons, the two measures nearly align. Gender differences trace to how family background shapes educational and occupational paths. Daughters pursue academic tracks and enter white-collar jobs with similar amenities at high rates regardless of background. Sons' paths are more stratified: those from disadvantaged families disproportionately follow vocational routes into blue-collar work, where both wages and amenities differ sharply from the professional jobs that advantaged sons obtain.

title: Digital Payment, Money Market Fund Competition, and Risk-Taking
affiliations: Gakushuin University

detail.title: Digital Payment, Money Market Fund Competition, and Risk-Taking
detail.abstract: Exploiting the expansion of China’s Yu’e Bao platform as a natural experiment, we find that digital payment integration enhances fund market power by reducing investor sensitivity to yields. This increased market power induces funds to make counterbalancing portfolio adjustments, including reallocating toward safer asset classes and extending portfolio maturity. Inclusion in the platform also reduces the absolute deviation between market and book value NAVs, indicating greater fund stability. Together, these findings provide novel evidence that digital payment integration acts as a stabilizing force in money markets by dampening competitive pressures that might otherwise incentivize excessive risk-taking.

title: Non-affiliated Distribution and Fund Performance:Evidence from Bank Wealth Management Funds in China

detail.title: Non-affiliated Distribution and Fund Performance:Evidence from Bank Wealth Management Funds in China
detail.abstract: Using the Measures for the Administration of Bank Wealth Management Funds Sales as an exogenous shock in fund distributions in Chinese BWM industry, we find that the increase in non-affiliated distribution brokers causally improves fund performance. The effect is more pronounced when the distribution broker possesses greater market power, when the fund issuer exhibits greater distribution dependence, and when horizontal competition is stronger between the distribution broker and fund issuer. Our findings indicate that non-affiliated distribution mitigates agency problems by providing both ex-ante effort-inducing and ex-post performance-monitoring, underscoring the role of non-affiliated distribution as an effective external governance mechanism.

title: Director Optimism: Should shareholders pay attention?
affiliations: James Madison University, University of Alabama - Culverhouse College of Business Administration and James Madison University

detail.title: Director Optimism: Should shareholders pay attention?
detail.abstract: We find evidence that directors’ favorable assessment of CEO ability, identified through their option exercise activity, accurately reflects future firm performance. When directors are optimistic, the likelihood of the forced CEO turnover is lower and the forced CEO turnover is less sensitive to firm stock performance. In addition, following periods of poor performance, firms with an optimistic board perform better than other firms. These results hold following two exogenous market-wide negative shocks to firm performance. Finally, optimistic directors’ trade-level profitability is higher. These findings indicate that director optimism reflects their private information rather than CEO entrenchment, suggesting that investors should pay attention to directors’ option exercise behavior.

title: Ambiguous Volatility, Asymmetric Information and Irreversible Investment
affiliations: Renmin University of China, Strathclyde Business School and Renmin University of China

detail.title: Ambiguous Volatility, Asymmetric Information and Irreversible Investment
detail.abstract: We develop a signaling game model of real investment with asymmetric information to examine the implications of ambiguity aversion on corporate investment dynamics and financing choices. Our analysis reveals that volatility ambiguity has a comparable yet more pronounced influence than asymmetric information, leading to heightened financing costs, decreased investment probabilities, and prompting non-participation investment decisions. This heightened ambiguity aversion escalates the likelihood of inefficient separating and pooling equilibria, ultimately resulting in a discernible welfare loss. The findings underscore the substantial impact of ambiguity aversion on strategic decision-making and equilibrium outcomes in the context of investment within environments characterized by information asymmetry and incomplete markets.

title: Regional Currency Overvaluation and Labor Market Rigidity
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE), Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE), Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), University of Melbourne and Peking University - School of Economics

detail.title: Regional Currency Overvaluation and Labor Market Rigidity
detail.abstract: We examine the issue of regional currency overvaluation within a large sovereign country marked by uneven economic growth across its regions. Regions with weaker economic fundamentals require a weaker currency, but a uniform exchange rate in a sovereign country prevents this adjustment, negatively impacting exports. While a more flexible labor market could help reduce costs, rising minimum wage standards contribute to labor market rigidity, hindering necessary changes. This combination of a uniform exchange rate, regional economic disparities, and an inflexible labor market ultimately undermines export competitiveness. Using detailed customs data from China, we document that the RMB is overvalued for regions with poor fundamentals. With rising minimum wage standards, these regions cannot reduce labor costs, leading to serious contractions in exports. This adverse effect is particularly pronounced in cities with elevated land prices and among firms with high labor intensity and poor performance.

title: Market Impacts and Unintended Consequences of Housing Assistance Policies with Price Thresholds
affiliations: National University of Singapore, Zicklin School of Business, Baruch College - The City University of New York and Deakin University - Department of Finance (Property and Real Estate)

detail.title: Market Impacts and Unintended Consequences of Housing Assistance Policies with Price Thresholds
detail.abstract: We find a housing assistance policy targeting at new homes priced up to $600,000 leads to substantial volume bunching just below $600,000, over 8 times counterfactual density. The surge in demand for policy-eligible homes results in an average overpricing of $4,000, offsetting up to 71% of received benefits, indicating considerable market distortions and price inflations. Policy-affected homes experience an average 25% reduction in area size and 57% higher likelihood of becoming rental investment properties in the long term, undermining the goal of boosting homeownership. Our findings shed light on the strategic market responses and negative externalities of macroprudential housing polices.

title: Data-Driven Financial Performance Analysis through Key Performance Indicators with Sensitivity and Predictive Insights: A Five-Year Study of a Public Sector IT Park
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Data-Driven Financial Performance Analysis through Key Performance Indicators with Sensitivity and Predictive Insights: A Five-Year Study of a Public Sector IT Park
detail.abstract:
The following study, “Data-Driven Financial Performance Analysis Through Key Performance Indicators with Sensitivity and Predictive Insights: A Five-Year Study of a Public Sector IT Park,” assesses the financial health and operational efficiency of the public sector IT Park through a data-centric analytical framework. Five years of audited financial statements (2019–2024) are studied to measure the performance of the organization based on key financial KPIs consisting of Net Surplus Margin, ROA, Current Ratio, and Interest Coverage Ratio. Descriptive analysis, sensitivity analysis, and predictive modeling have been conducted using Excel, Power BI, and Python.

The results indicate that the IT Park witnessed robust growth in surplus margins between 2019–20 and 2022–23 on the back of good cost control and stable revenue, succeeded by a significant decline in 2023–24 induced by increased depreciation, exceptional expenses, and higher administrative costs. Sensitivity analysis indicates that occupancy and revenue variations significantly impact net surplus and, therefore, represent critical performance drivers. Predictive analysis shows modest future improvement, supporting long-term strategic planning.

The study concludes that the integration of KPI assessment with sensitivity and forecasting tools promotes financial transparency and facilitates evidence-based decision-making in public sector infrastructure institutions. Recommendations focus on enhancing cost management, improving asset utilization, diversifying revenue streams, and perfecting forecasting practices for long-term financial stability.

title: Does Sustainable Investing Spread Through Social Networks?
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Nanyang Business School, Division of Banking & Finance, Students

detail.title: Does Sustainable Investing Spread Through Social Networks?
detail.abstract: This paper examines how peer effects in social networks shape institutional investors' decisions on sustainable investing. Using the U.S. county-level Social Connectedness Index, I document that when institutional investors experience natural disasters and subsequently adjust their portfolios toward more sustainable stocks, other institutional investors in socially connected areas unaffected by these disasters exhibit similar sustainability tilts. Sustainable stocks that are heavily purchased by institutions “socially” exposed to climate risks experience predictable reversals of future returns. Low-skill and small institutional investors are more susceptible to such green social contagion. Evidence from newly introduced direct flights, which provides plausibly exogenous variation in social connectedness, also confirms the diffusion of sustainable investing.

title: When Help Can Hurt: Effects of Government Subsidies on Cost of Debt – Beyond the Mean
affiliations: , Marquette University - Department of Finance, University of New Orleans - College of Business Administration - Department of Economics and Finance and Ball State University - Miller College of Business

detail.title: When Help Can Hurt: Effects of Government Subsidies on Cost of Debt – Beyond the Mean
detail.abstract: Government subsidies have long shaped the development of U.S. industries, in both stable periods and economic crises. Using a comprehensive database of local, State, and Federal programs from 2001-2022, this study examines how subsidies influence firms’ cost of debt. While conventional OLS estimates suggest non-tax subsidies reduce borrowing costs, distributional analysis reveals notable heterogeneity. Tax-based subsidies are consistently linked to higher debt costs, regardless of firms’ credit strength, and the apparent benefits of non-tax subsidies largely vanish once cross-industry differences are considered. Two quasi-natural experiments, the 2009 ARRA program and the 2020 COVID-19 interventions; reinforce these patterns. ARRA support eased financing for constrained firms but raised costs for stronger borrowers, and the COVID-19 subsidy slowdown increased debt costs across the board. Overall, the findings show that subsidy effects are asymmetric and risk-dependent, highlighting the need for more targeted policy design. This study provides the first distribution-based evidence of such heterogeneity.

title: US Labor Market Conditions and Migration: A Reassessment of Bahar (2025)

detail.title: US Labor Market Conditions and Migration: A Reassessment of Bahar (2025)

detail.abstract: Bahar (2025) argues that there is a long-term cointegrating relationship between US job vacancies and Southwest border crossings. We show that his conclusion is based on a misspecified Engle-Granger test applied to first differences. Once the Engle-Granger test is correctly applied to levels, evidence for a cointegrating relationship vanishes, invalidating the paper's approach to estimating short-and long-run elasticities. Bahar's approach is therefore uninformative about the relationship between US labor market conditions and migration.

title: Deposit Specialization and Lending Behavior
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York University (NYU) - New York University and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Deposit Specialization and Lending Behavior

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1175
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine how banks' depositor composition shapes lending behavior, using granular supervisory data on deposits, loans, and securities for the largest U.S. banks. Classifying banks by depositor specialization, we find persistent differences in funding that translate to differences in asset allocations. Retail-depositor oriented banks hold longer-maturity loans and conduct more real estate lending, while corporate-and NBFI-oriented banks, whose funding is more volatile, hold shorter loans and liquid securities. Loan-level analyses show that stable funding is associated with lower rates, longer maturities, and larger loans. Growth in deposits is allocated differently depending on the depositor specialization of the bank, something we can explore using exogenous deposit growth during COVID.

title: Post-Conflict Recovery and Peacebuilding in Southern Africa
affiliations: IIE ADvTECH and Durban University of Technology (DUT)

detail.title: Post-Conflict Recovery and Peacebuilding in Southern Africa
detail.abstract: This study explores post-conflict recovery and peacebuilding in Southern Africa, focusing on the strategies and challenges faced by nations emerging from periods of violence and instability. The region has a complex history characterized by protracted conflicts, including civil wars, ethnic tensions, and political strife, which have profoundly affected social cohesion and economic development. As countries such as Mozambique, Angola, and Zimbabwe strive for stability, understanding the dynamics of post-conflict recovery is crucial for fostering longterm peace and resilience. This systematic qualitative method aims to investigate to explore post-conflict recovery and peacebuilding in Southern Africa. The methodology involved a structured approach gathering and analysing qualitative data from relevant literature, and expert opinions. Selection of articles focused on peer-reviewed 37 articles from 1996 to 2021 that discuss post-conflict recovery and peacebuilding in Southern Africa. Data was categorised as specific recovery strategies, such as disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration (DDR) programs, and the effectiveness of truth and reconciliation commissions (Galtung, 1996). This systematic approach aimed to provide insights into the impact of post-conflict recovery and peacebuilding in Southern Africa. The findings highlight a critical interplay between grassroots initiatives and national policies in shaping recovery processes. Successful peacebuilding efforts are found to hinge on inclusive governance, community-led reconciliation programs, and economic revitalization strategies that address the root causes of conflict. However, the study also identifies significant challenges, such as persistent inequalities, weak institutional capacities, and the lingering effects of trauma that can hinder recovery efforts. Ultimately, this research emphasizes the importance of holistic approaches that integrate social, economic, and political dimensions in post-conflict contexts. By providing a nuanced understanding of the complexities of recovery and peacebuilding in Southern Africa, the study aims to inform policies and practices that promote sustainable peace, social justice, and development in the region.

title: Going Online or Falling Behind: Digitalization and Firm Performance during COVID-19
affiliations: University of Shkodra,  and

detail.title: Going Online or Falling Behind: Digitalization and Firm Performance during COVID-19
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between enterprise digitalisation and firm performance during the COVID-19 pandemic, using firm-level evidence from Albania. Drawing on data from the World Bank Enterprise Survey (2019) and the COVID-19 followup survey (2020), the analysis investigates whether different forms of digitalisation helped firms adjust to the crisis and sustain economic activity. Digitalisation is measured through three dimensions: increased online business activity, the use of firm websites, and the adoption of remote working arrangements. Firm performance is assessed in terms of sales growth, employment growth, and production or service adjustments during the pandemic. The results show that only revenue-oriented digitalisation, specifically the initiation or expansion of online business activity, has a positive and statistically significant effect on firm performance across all outcome measures. In contrast, the mere presence of a website or the adoption of remote work arrangements does not yield significant performance gains. These findings suggest that digital tools contribute to firm resilience during economic shocks only when they directly support market access and sales, rather than serving purely informational or organisational functions. By providing micro-level evidence from a small transition economy with relatively low digital intensity, this study contributes to the emerging literature on crisis-driven digital transformation and highlights important policy implications for supporting effective, rather than symbolic, digitalisation among firms.

title: An Exercise in Floor-Constrained Capitalism
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: An Exercise in Floor-Constrained Capitalism
detail.abstract: I formalize a welfare argument for floor-constrained capitalism, with an exogenous welfare floor but very minimal regulation. Here, credible exit options constrain exploitative bargaining without requiring microregulation, because agents can just leave transactions that push them below the guaranteed baseline. I show this configuration wins in both laissez-faire systems (where exit becomes non-credible and bargaining power concentrates) and very regulated capitalism (where compliance costs scale superlinearly with regulatory scope). The proof turns on three claims: markets aggregate dispersed information more efficiently than centralized planning, the welfare floor automates labor standards with reservation utility effects, and less governance avoids the deadweight losses that compound as rule systems interact. Obviously this is a theoretical exercise with some heroic assumptions, but if the logic holds, the optimal system might look less like a tradeoff between markets and regulation and more like strong floors plus strategic minimalism everywhere else.

title: An Interval-based Composite Indexing Method for Measuring Multidimensional Poverty: Introducing Santigwar Approach
affiliations: University of the Philippines, Los Baños - University of the Philippines Los Banos and University of the Philippines, Los Baños - University of the Philippines Los Banos

detail.title: An Interval-based Composite Indexing Method for Measuring Multidimensional Poverty: Introducing Santigwar Approach
detail.abstract: This work addresses the challenges of measuring and alleviating poverty, particularly in the poorest regions. Current poverty metrics are limited and suffer from drawbacks, making it difficult for policymakers to target poverty alleviation efforts effectively. The Santigwar model is introduced as a more effective measure, incorporating multiple constructs and indicators to predict and score composite poverty. By standardizing and decomposing data, it provides policymakers with valuable insights for developing intervention programs. This comprehensive approach measures poverty accurately and support economic development. The models presented can be replicated or reused by researchers worldwide to assist impoverished communities in improving their well-being.

title: Agrarian Governance – The Case of Bulgaria
affiliations: Institute of Agricultural Economics

detail.title: Agrarian Governance – The Case of Bulgaria

declarations.ethicsApproval: na
declarations.funderStatement: This study is funded by the Bulgarian Science Fund, the project "Agricultural land, green transformation, energy transition, digital environment", Contract No КП-06-Н96/2, 9.12.2025.

detail.abstract:
The term governance is widely used in a number of scientific disciplines, as well as by international, state, business, non-governmental, etc. organizations. The interdisciplinary New Institutional Economics has contributed greatly to the modern understanding of the nature and factors of governance in general, and of governance in individual areas of social activity and levels of analysis – from the governance of individual transactions to the governance of global affairs. Almost ninety years after the “discovery” of transaction costs by Coase (1937) and the “reasons” for the existence of economic organizations of different types, today this “new” methodology is an integral part of the general (mainstream) economic theory and analysis. Of course, Williamson (1985) - in operationalizing this concept, and North (1991) - in revealing the role of institutions in economic development, significantly contributed to the development of the New Institutional Economics. Many other economists have also made a great contribution to the development of this new "branch" of economic science, which has been well summarized by Furubotn and Richter (2005) and Ménard and Shirley (2022).
The author of this study was among the first to adapt the achievements of the New Institutional Economics in the analysis of agrarian governance and institutional modernization in Bulgaria (Bachev, 1996) and elsewhere (Bachev, 1995). Over the past three decades, Bulgarian economists have made numerous publications with analyses of the forms, factors, effectiveness and evolution of the governance of the main types of agrarian transactions, farmer organizations, and levels of governance during the period of transformation, pre-accession and full membership of the country in the European Union (https://agro-governance.alle.bg/#). Here we would like to underline our close cooperation with the leading scholars in the institutional analysis of agrarian contracts and organizations from the University of Missouri in the USA, which began in 1992 and has been deepening to the present day. We are especially grateful to Michael Cook and Michael Sykuta for their training, inspiration, continuous support and long-term cooperation.
The paper presents the results of current research in the field of agrarian governance in Bulgaria. Without claiming to be comprehensive, it provides an idea of the Bulgarian experience in agrarian governance, and of the modest Bulgarian contribution to the implementation of the institutional analysis of the modes and mechanisms of agrarian governance.
First, a holistic approach to understanding and analysing agrarian governance is presented. Then, the economic role of agrarian contracts is revealed, their types are classified, and an approach to assessing their effectiveness is presented. This is followed by an assessment of the quality of the system of agrarian governance in Bulgaria at present stage of development. Then, an analysis of the governance and contractual structures of major functional areas of Bulgarian farms is made. Then, the forms, factors and effectiveness of land and labour supplies in Bulgarian farms are identified. The identification of modes, factors and efficiency of the provision of eco-system services by the Bulgarian farms follows. After that the levels and evolution of governance efficiency of Bulgarian farms are evaluated. Then a holistic assessment of comparative and absolute competitiveness of Bulgarian farms is made. Finally, the state, evolution, efficiency and factors of governance of agricultural inclusion in sustainable wastewater management in Bulgaria is presented.
The paper is of interest to a wide range of readers - researchers, teachers, students, managers of agricultural holdings, agro-companies and cooperatives, heads and specialists of state, international and professional organizations, investors, politicians, interest groups and the general public.

title: The Impact of ACA Medicaid Expansion on U.S. Fertility Rates
affiliations: Wellesley College - Department of Economics, Wellesley College - Department of Economics and Wellesley College - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Impact of ACA Medicaid Expansion on U.S. Fertility Rates

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We did not have any personal or financial relationships with other individuals or organizations that may have influenced or could be perceived to have influenced our study.
declarations.funderStatement: We were not funded for this research.

detail.abstract:
In our current policy landscape, declining national fertility rates and growing uncertainty around reproductive services have raised significant concerns. Thus, high-quality, affordable reproductive healthcare access is particularly critical. We must move beyond rhetoric and political narratives to understand how data and empirical evidence can inform the understanding of what influences reproductive health outcomes. This study examines the impact of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Medicaid Expansion on fertility rates in the United States by tracking births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 44.

Young women from low-income demographics face the greatest barriers to accessing consistent reproductive, prenatal, and maternal care. Medicaid, which pays for 42% of U.S. births, plays a particularly critical role in shaping these outcomes. The 2012 Supreme Court decision made Medicaid expansion optional, creating variation across states and a subsequent natural experiment. Starting in 2014, some states immediately expanded, while several expanded in later years, and some never expanded. This staggered rollout allows economists to compare outcomes in expansion states with outcomes in non-expansion states.

We merged CDC natality data with Kaiser Family Foundation Medicaid expansion data, forming a panel of all 50 states from 2007 through 2020, resulting in 714 state-year observations. Using a difference-in-differences approach and event-study method, we first compared fertility rates before and after expansion, controlling for state and year fixed effects. Then, we included additional demographic controls like marital status, education, income, and age.

Our results found no significant relationship between Medicaid expansion and fertility rates. All coefficients in the pre-expansion period are small and not statistically different from zero, confirming our confidence in the parallel trends assumption. Post-expansion coefficients remain close to zero with wide confidence intervals, suggesting Medicaid expansion did not create a meaningful shift in fertility rates when looking at the policy effect five years after implementation. Several factors may explain our findings, including increased access to long-acting reversible contraceptives, nationwide declining fertility trends, macroeconomic factors from the 2007 recession, and variation in how states implemented expansion. While we do not find evidence that Medicaid expansion altered fertility rates, our results contribute to understanding how major health policy shifts intersect with women's reproductive choices.

title: Household Borrowing and Monetary Policy Transmission: Post-Pandemic Insights from Nine European Credit Registers

detail.title: Household Borrowing and Monetary Policy Transmission: Post-Pandemic Insights from Nine European Credit Registers

keywords: monetary policy transmission; household borrowing; credit registers; interest rate pass-through; cross-country heterogeneity

publicationDetails.journalName: National Bank of Belgium Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study heterogeneity in households’ credit across nine European countries (Belgium, Spain, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Portugal, and Slovakia) during 2022-2024 using granular credit register data. We first document substantial between- and within-country variation in mortgage and consumer lending by borrower age, loan maturity, and interest rate fixation. We then quantify the pass-through of the ECB’s recent tightening cycle to household borrowing costs and assess its heterogeneous impact across households. Pass-through is nearly complete for mortgages (around 0.9) but considerably weaker for consumer credit (around 0.4). While mortgage pass-through is relatively homogeneous across countries, consumer credit shows pronounced cross-country differences that cannot be explained by borrower or loan characteristics. Younger households face stronger mortgage pass-through but weaker consumer credit pass-through relative to older borrowers, and longer maturities are associated with stronger pass-through in both credit markets.

title: A Study on the Interactive Mechanisms of Work Pressure, Health Risks, and Social Evaluation Among Food Delivery Riders in the Platform Economy
affiliations: Central South University,  and Hunan University

detail.title: A Study on the Interactive Mechanisms of Work Pressure, Health Risks, and Social Evaluation Among Food Delivery Riders in the Platform Economy
detail.abstract: Food delivery riders play an increasingly important role in urban traffic systems but face elevated safety and health risks due to high work intensity, time pressure, and algorithmic management. While prior studies based on the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) model have mainly examined risky riding behaviors, the psychological mechanisms linking working conditions to health risks remain insufficiently understood, particularly the role of social identity. Drawing on the JD-R model and Social Identity Theory, this study investigates how job demands and job resources affect work stress and health risks among Chinese food delivery riders and examines the moderating role of social identity. A cross-sectional survey of 315 riders from multiple Chinese cities was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling. The results show that job demands significantly increase work stress, whereas job resources reduce it. Work stress is positively associated with health risks and partially mediates the effects of job demands and job resources on health outcomes. Moreover, perceived occupational prestige and public opinion evaluation weaken the stress-inducing effect of job demands, while public opinion evaluation strengthens the stress-buffering effect of job resources. These findings highlight work stress as a key psychological mechanism shaping health-related risks and provide insights for improving rider safety in urban traffic environments.

title: Can You Take Me Higher? No. 110, Drug Decriminalization, and Residential Real Estate Prices
affiliations: Wenzhou-Kean University and Nanjing University - School of Business

detail.title: Can You Take Me Higher? No. 110, Drug Decriminalization, and Residential Real Estate Prices
detail.abstract: Researchers in criminology, law, and economics claim significant social improvements from drug decriminalization. This paper questions those claims. While drug decriminalization measures may improve some observable economic metrics, residential real estate prices ultimately reflect the overall desirability of living in a jurisdiction without penalties for drug use. Using the mass decriminalization of narcotics in Oregon as a natural experiment in a differences-in-differences setting, we show that housing prices decline dramatically and persistently when drug decriminalization becomes imminent. While narcotics decriminalization may have positive effects observable by economists, less observable measures of sentiment ultimately show souring sentiment among residents and investors.

title: Who Gains from Drone Integration in Instant Delivery? Market Expansion, Pricing, and Welfare in a Spatial Delivery Market
affiliations: ,  Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and  Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

detail.title: Who Gains from Drone Integration in Instant Delivery? Market Expansion, Pricing, and Welfare in a Spatial Delivery Market
detail.abstract:
We study when and from who drone integration creates value in the instant delivery market.  

Existing research has largely concentrated on operational challenges, leaving the strategic and economic implications insufficiently understood. We develop a tractable spatial-economic model in which drones operate alongside crowd-source couriers, capturing endogenous pricing, courier supply and delivery efficiency under perfect competition, monopoly and Bertrand duopoly. 

The model yields structural conditions governing drone entry, market coverage and pricing competition. Our key insight is that drones generate value primarily through spatial market expansion, rather than marginal cost reductions. Whenever drones obtain a positive share under equilibrium conditions, a bi-modal system using both drones and human couriers outperforms single-mode ones in market coverage, platform profit, and social welfare. Delivery-time unreliability for couriers further lowers the distance threshold at which drones become the preferred mode, expanding its equilibrium share and amplifies efficiency gains. Numerical simulations based on real delivery data support these findings and show that customers, especially those in remote areas and with high values, are the primary beneficiaries of drone integration.

title: From Macaulay to Modernity: The Historical Trajectory of English and the Two-Language Theory in India

detail.title: From Macaulay to Modernity: The Historical Trajectory of English and the Two-Language Theory in India
detail.abstract: This essay examines India's enduring dependence on English as an official language through the lens of decolonisation theory. It traces the transformation of English from a colonial instrument to a postcolonial necessity that continues to perpetuate epistemic hierarchies and constrain India's soft power. The study advances a two-language theory, proposing a gradual transition from English as an official language to an indigenous Indian one through a democratic and federative process. By reimagining governance, education, and diplomacy in indigenous languages, it positions linguistic indigenisation as central to India's pursuit of cultural sovereignty. The essay concludes that genuine modernity lies in reclaiming the capacity to think, govern, and communicate in languages rooted in India's own civilisational heritage.

title: Can Robotization Save Jobs from Slowbalization? *
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management and Jinan University

detail.title: Can Robotization Save Jobs from Slowbalization? *
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how robot adoption interacts with trade slowdowns to impact local labor markets in China. We highlight the role of industrial robots in mitigating the adverse impact of export slowdown on the local labor market. Employing a Bartik-style instrumental variable approach, we construct a prefecture-level measure of robot adoption and find that an interquartile increase in robot installations leads to a relative increase in the employment of around 0.16 percentage points, holding the Chinese export shock constant at its mean value of 61.42 dollars per worker. Our evidence suggests that firms' adoption of robots helps offset employment losses from trade slowdown by increasing domestic sales. Moreover, this adjustment is accompanied by an increase in local consumption, and coincides with shifts in employment structure that disproportionately benefit highly educated workers, as they are less vulnerable to automation.

title: The Financial Accounting Model from a System Dynamics’ Perspective
affiliations: Maastricht Accounting and Auditing Research and Education Center (MARC)

detail.title: The Financial Accounting Model from a System Dynamics’ Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: ABSTRACT We examined the hypothesis that boredom is likely to occur when opportunity costs are high; that is, when there is a high potential value of engaging in activities other than the researcher-assigned activity. To this end, participants were either placed in a room with many possible affordances (e.g. a laptop, puzzle, etc.; affordances condition; n = 121), or they were ushered into an empty room (control condition; n = 107). In both conditions participants were instructed to entertain themselves with only their thoughts (hence, participants in the affordances condition were to refrain from engaging with the available options). As predicted, participants in the affordances condition reported higher levels of boredom compared with those in the control condition. Results suggest that under some conditions, environments that afford alternative activities may be more boring than those that are void of such activities.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the foundation of the financial accounting model. We examine the properties of the accounting equation as the principal algorithm for the design and the development of a System Dynamics model. Key to the perspective is the foundational requirement that resolves the temporal conflict that resides in a stock and flow model. Through formal analysis the accounting equation is redefined as a cybernetic model by expressing the temporal and dynamic properties of its terms. Articulated in that form the accounting equation is enabled to be defined as a dynamic stock and flow model expressing the two dimensions of the double-entry accounting system. With that formal foundation it is argued that the accounting model is capable to simulate financial dynamics as well as be integrated with models that express operational and world dynamics. Thus we prove that it is possible to design and build a dynamic business model that can meet requirements of management accounting (ex ante, before the fact) as well as financial accounting (ex post, after the fact). We conclude that the dynamic accounting model can be made relevant for strategic planning and control purposes and be integrated within a System Dynamics model designed for such purposes.

title: The Economics of Climate Innovation: Technology, Climate Policy, and the Clean Energy Transition
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Geography and Environment and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: The Economics of Climate Innovation: Technology, Climate Policy, and the Clean Energy Transition
detail.abstract:
This chapter examines the economics of climate innovation and its role in the clean technology transition. It outlines the incentives, market failures, and policy levers that shape the development and diffusion of clean technologies; traces global patterns in technology development and deployment; and highlights frontier challenges and open questions related to climate adaptation, critical mineral supply chains, artificial intelligence, and geopolitics. The analysis explores the role of effective climate policy, stressing the relevance of coordinated approaches that match instruments to technology maturity and local context.

title: Academic Time Constraints and Adolescent Physical Activity: A Natural Experiment from China's Double Reduction Policy
affiliations: Guangzhou Nanfang College, Guangzhou Nanfang College and Guangzhou Nanfang College

detail.title: Academic Time Constraints and Adolescent Physical Activity: A Natural Experiment from China's Double Reduction Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study complies with the Declaration of Helsinki. The data used in this study were obtained from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), which was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Peking University (Approval No.: IRB00001052-14010). All participants provided informed consent before the interviews.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Background: Approximately 81% of adolescents worldwide fail to meet physical activity guidelines, with academic burden frequently cited as a barrier. However, existing evidence relies on observational studies that cannot exclude confounding. Time-use epidemiology shows sedentary behavior and physical activity are only weakly correlated (r=-0.108), challenging time-substitution assumptions, yet causal evidence from exogenous shocks remains lacking.

Methods: This study employs China's 2021 "Double Reduction" policy as a quasi-natural experiment, using difference-in-differences to assess causal effects of academic time constraints on adolescent physical activity. The policy restricted extracurricular tutoring for compulsory education students (grades 1-9) but not high school students (grades 10-12). Using China Family Panel Studies data (2020-2022), the sample included 2,848 observations from 1,424 individuals (1,229 treatment, 195 control). Identification was validated through placebo testing (2018-2020, p=0.16).

Results: The policy reduced tutoring time by 2.85 hours/week (66% decrease, p=0.026) and increased physical activity scores by 0.44 points (0-7 scale, 19% increase, p=0.044). However, individual-level tutoring reductions showed no correlation with physical activity increases (r=0.002, p=0.75). This null finding aligns with Pearson et al.'s (2014) meta-analysis but provides first causal evidence under exogenous policy shock.

Conclusion: Academic time constraints causally limit adolescent physical activity, yet time release alone does not trigger automatic substitution at the individual level. Significant group-level effects without individual-level mechanisms suggest policy operates through school institutional changes rather than household time reallocation. Promoting adolescent physical activity requires environmental support beyond reducing academic burden.

title: Gender Trade Gap
affiliations: University of Sussex Business School

detail.title: Gender Trade Gap
detail.abstract: Using novel data on CEO gender information from millions of US establishments between 2010 and 2021, I document a novel gender gap that I call the gender trade gap: establishments and firms headed by women are less likely to engage in exporting and importing compared to their male counterparts. This could lead to significant gender gaps in other outcomes since international trade often spurs the growth of businesses. The gap is observed in every industry, county, and employment size group. Controlling for a variety of characteristics such as industry, region, employment, and age does not eliminate the gap. In fact, the gap is significantly present even if establishment fixed effects, year fixed effects, and employment are included in multi-year data. Moreover, the gap persists across establishments within the same firm.

title: Predictive Structure and Observer-Space Geometry: Foundations of a Generative Theory of Prediction

detail.title: Predictive Structure and Observer-Space Geometry: Foundations of a Generative Theory of Prediction

detail.abstract: We develop a structural theoretical framework for predictive distinctions-differences among possible futures that matter for what the universe tends to do next-and the observer-space organisation they induce. Observers arise as stabilised compressions of these distinctions under finite-resource constraints, giving rise to an abstract observer space organised through relational rather than metric structure. Neighbourhoods, soft directions, and stiff axes emerge as relational invariants, forming what we call conceptual predictive geometry. This geometry makes adaptation, multiplicity, and reflexivity intelligible as movements, distributions, and deformations within observer space. The framework introduces no metrics, algorithms, manifolds, or update rules; its contribution is structural rather than operational, articulating the minimal organisational conditions under which observers, predictive vocabularies, and higher-order patterns become possible. This manuscript is not a survey or position paper; it presents a structural theoretical framework and does not express programmatic or evaluative positions. It provides conceptual foundations intended to support later technical elaborations and domain-specific developments.

title: Human Capital and Development
affiliations: London School of Economics, Stockholm University and Yale University

detail.title: Human Capital and Development
detail.abstract:
Human capital is central to efforts to promote growth, convergence, and the elimination of poverty. Drawing on the seminal macroeconomic frameworks by Nelson-Phelps, Lucas and subsequent developments, alongside macro and microeconomic evidence, we examine the role of human capital in driving innovation and growth. We highlight how different types of human capital, characterized by education level, matter in different stages of development. Despite documented increases in years of schooling, the world’s poorest regions still see stagnating outcomes in learning and education quality, potentially creating poverty traps where investments in neither physical nor human capital materialize. We discuss obstacles to human capital accumulation through a simple analytical framework and present evidence from randomized interventions spanning early childhood programs to school-age initiatives, assessing policies that can effectively remove barriers to skill acquisition and establish foundations for sustained growth.

title: Connected for Better or Worse? The Role of Production Networks in Financial Crises
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), University of Florida - Department of Economics, University of Virginia - Darden School of Business and Latin American Center for Economic and Social Policies (CLAPES UC), Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile

detail.title: Connected for Better or Worse? The Role of Production Networks in Financial Crises
detail.abstract:
We study how production networks shape the severity of Sudden Stops. We build a small open economy model with collateral constraints and input–output linkages, derive a sufficient statistic that maps network structure into the amplification of tradable shocks, and show that a planner optimally introduces sectoral wedges to reduce amplification. Using OECD input–output data and Sudden Stop episodes, we document systematic network differences between emerging and advanced economies and show they predict crisis severity. A calibrated three-sector DSGE model disciplined by these differences reveals that endowing an advanced economy with an emerging-market production network moves most of the way toward the observed emerging–advanced Sudden Stop gap.

title: Women's Power in the Household
affiliations: Princeton University and Stanford University

detail.title: Women's Power in the Household
detail.abstract:
We examine women's household power in low- and middle-income countries, synthesizing theoretical frameworks and empirical evidence on its measurement, determinants, and consequences. We define women's household power as their influence over household choices, distinguishing it from broader empowerment concepts. We review economic models, including unitary, collective, and bargaining frameworks, and map these to empirical approaches. We then discuss measurement methods such as structural estimation of consumption allocation, survey measures, and laboratory experiments. On the determinants of women's power, we find that some approaches, such as transfers targeted to women, show mixed results, while others, such as increasing women's control over their earnings, show clearer positive impacts. On the effects of women's power, we pay special attention to children's human capital. Few studies provide strong evidence that mothers invest more in children than fathers do, but collectively the evidence suggests such an effect. We conclude by highlighting research and methodological gaps.

title: Development Hazard: Modeling the Spillover Effects of Migrant Youth Marginalization in Host Economies

detail.title: Development Hazard: Modeling the Spillover Effects of Migrant Youth Marginalization in Host Economies
detail.abstract: Migration is often celebrated for fostering economic development through remittances, labor mobility, and human capital transfer. However, this paper introduces the concept of Development Hazard-a systemic risk arising from the marginalization of migrants in host economies due to persistent structural barriers. This study develops a formal model linking migrant volume (M), integration barriers (B), and inclusion outcomes (I), demonstrating that the marginal risk of exclusion rises with structural barriers but plateaus at high levels. Using OECD panel data based on panel data of African youth migrants in OECD countries from 2015-2023"). We empirically validate the model and simulate policy interventions across Germany, Tunisia, and Sweden. Results highlight that reducing structural barriers yields superior development outcomes compared to migration restrictions, especially when targeting youth migrants. We argue for a shift from volume centric policies to integration-centric strategies as the key to converting migration into a sustainable development asset.

title: The Long Run Economic Effects of Medical Innovation and the Role of Opportunities
affiliations: IZA Institute of Labor Economics, University of Oxford - Department of Economics and University of Pennsylvania - Perelman School of Medicine

detail.title: The Long Run Economic Effects of Medical Innovation and the Role of Opportunities

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We leverage the introduction of the first antibiotic therapies in 1937 to examine the long-run effects of early-childhood pneumonia on adult educational attainment, employment, income, and work-related disability. Using census data, we document large average improvements across all outcomes, alongside substantial heterogeneity by gender and race. Among women, health gains led to changes in marriage and fertility that partially offset their labor market improvements. Among Black Americans, we uncover a pronounced gradient linked to systemic racial discrimination in the pre-Civil Rights era: individuals born in more discriminatory Jim Crow states realized much smaller gains than those born in less discriminatory states, despite larger reductions in pneumonia exposure. There is no similar gradient among white Americans. Together, these findings highlight the central role of institutional environments in shaping whether investments in early-life health translate into long-run socioeconomic gains.

title: Open Devices and Slices: Evidence From Wi-Fi Equipment
affiliations: Boston College, University of Pavia and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: Open Devices and Slices: Evidence From Wi-Fi Equipment
detail.abstract:
The study examines the quasi-natural experiments provided by the staggered introduction of open drivers in the supply chains for routers. It is rare to observe components become open and measure whether openness generates a statistical impact on more products and innovative products. This study collects novel data on all routers and subcomponents introduced between 2000 and 2018, characterizing each firm's position in a supply chain as either an upstream component provider or a downstream router assembler. Following prior literature, openness influences a firm's ability to negotiate with current and potential partners, which is labeled as autonomy. Evidence suggests that openness enhances supplier autonomy, increases the introduction of new products, and leads to a greater number of products located closer to the technical frontier. These estimates suggest that openness increased product introductions by enlarging the options available to component suppliers. The largest component suppliers benefited from greater sales, and no evidence indicates that openness aided entrants, small firms, or assemblers.

detail.abstract: Minimum wages are found to have an inconclusive impact on poverty. Using China’s individual-level panel dataset combined with county-level minimum wages, our paper shows that minimum wages have a moderate yet sustained effect on poverty reduction. The results show a two-sided effect: higher minimum wages help pull some workers out of poverty, while simultaneously pushing others in. This dynamic of larger “pulling” effects being counterbalanced by smaller “pushing” effects explains why existing studies often find that minimum wages have a negligible or minimal impact on poverty reduction. Notably, the poverty reduction effect is most pronounced for female workers.

title: Music Metadata Minefield: Prior Initiatives, Interoperability and How to let GenAI's Copyright Traces Transpire

detail.title: Music Metadata Minefield: Prior Initiatives, Interoperability and How to let GenAI's Copyright Traces Transpire
detail.abstract: This chapter shows that music industry and EU Initiatives at the start of the online era for music consumption between the early 2000s and the early 2010s, aiming for centralised copyright databases, failed in part due misaligned remuneration systems and economic priorities. Some challenges present since those early years have remained, while new ones have emerged with the advent of music streaming, and more recently also with GenAI music tools and services. Decentralised solutions also still have to grapple with metadata design challenges for attaining music metadata interoperability, generally with regard to domain specificity, granularity and provenance. The transparency obligations in Article 50 and 53(1)(d) of the AI Act as of yet do not provide sufficient practical, enforceable rules that can improve metadata interoperability for GenAI music in the (European) music industry, also not through the explanations and guidance given in the First Draft Code of Practice in relation to Article 50 or the Explanatory Notice and Template for Article 53.

title: Fiscal Geometry under Closed Axes: Clarifying SITI and ZITI as Theme-Constrained Readings on the X-Y Plane

detail.title: Fiscal Geometry under Closed Axes: Clarifying SITI and ZITI as Theme-Constrained Readings on the X-Y Plane
detail.abstract:
This working paper clarifies the definitional boundary between SITI and ZITI within Fiscal Geometry (FG) without introducing any additional axes beyond the X-Y plane. The paper treats "themes" not as new dimensions, but as constraint conditions that produce slice-style readings of the same underlying interaction record space. Under this closed-axes grammar, SITI is specified as a high-resolution slice reading that renders localized structure under a controlled thematic constraint, while ZITI is specified as a theme-constrained reading that organizes visibility around a coherent topic without altering the coordinate system itself. 

The paper explains why adding axes destabilizes comparability and model-readability, especially for downstream AI mapping and reuse. A minimal tolerance analogy is introduced only as an explanatory layer: in running systems, non-zero structural clearance functions as an operational margin rather than a compromise, helping absorb heat, load variation, and stress concentration. 

The paper makes no causal, normative, or policy claims. Its contribution is definitional stability: a reusable reference vocabulary, a separation of roles between SITI and ZITI, and a closed-axes specification that preserves FG as a machine-readable representation layer on the X-Y plane.

title: A Lifecycle Estimator of Intergenerational Income Mobility
affiliations: Instituto de Ensino e Pesquisa (INSPER), Stockholm University - Swedish Institute for Social Research (SOFI) and Charles III University of Madrid

detail.title: A Lifecycle Estimator of Intergenerational Income Mobility

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Lacking lifetime income data, most intergenerational mobility estimates are subject to lifecycle bias. Using long income series from Sweden and the US, we illustrate that standard correction methods struggle to account for one important property of income processes: children from affluent families experience faster income growth, even conditional on their own characteristics. We propose a lifecycle estimator that captures this pattern and performs well across different settings. We apply the estimator to study mobility trends, including for recent cohorts that could not be considered in prior work. Despite rising income inequality, intergenerational mobility remained largely stable in both countries.

title: Accounting For Accountability: Incorporating Oversight Into The Section 139l Partial Interest Income Tax Exclusion For Lenders

detail.title: Accounting For Accountability: Incorporating Oversight Into The Section 139l Partial Interest Income Tax Exclusion For Lenders
detail.abstract: Farmers, ranchers, rural residents, and their businesses currently face a wide range of issues, such as high costs of inputs, low market prices, and supply chain issues from uncertain trade conditions. High interest rates further increase the financial pressure on those individuals by raising the expense of a loan to purchase property, equipment, or other capital assets. As an incentive for lending institutions to make long-term rural and agricultural loans, Congress passed 26 U.S.C. Section 139L on July 4, 2025 as a provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Section 139L provides a twenty-five percent gross interest income exclusion to qualified lenders on qualified real estate loans. Congress passed Section 139L so that lenders would lower the cost of borrowing for their rural and agricultural customers; however, the Act does not contain any requirement to pass down the tax benefit through lower interest rates or any other service in accordance with that goal. This Article will propose an amendment to Section 139L to require lenders to provide savings and aid to borrowers and to report progress on that initiative to their supervisory agency. In addition, the amendment authorizes regulatory agencies to oversee the lenders in carrying out those initiatives and to revoke eligibility for the tax exclusion from lenders who do not comply with the statute's action or reporting requirements.

title: Global Climate Risk and Investment Attractiveness: The Role of the Belt and Road Initiative

detail.title: Global Climate Risk and Investment Attractiveness: The Role of the Belt and Road Initiative
detail.abstract: This study investigates how overseas climate risk shapes corporate foreign direct investment and explores potential mitigation strategies. Using a firmcountry dual-level dataset, we find that host country climate risk significantly inhibits foreign direct investment. Mechanism analysis reveals that this inhibition operates by eroding corporate resource allocation efficiency. Furthermore, we examine the role of institutional and policy environments as protective constraints. While host-country institutional quality offers a static buffer, our analysis using the Difference-inDifferences with Multiple Time Periods (CSDID) demonstrates that the Belt and Road Initiative acts as a powerful dynamic policy shock. The results confirm that the Belt and Road Initiative effectively promotes foreign direct investment, serving as a critical "policy antidote" that enables firms to navigate climate uncertainties.

title: The Role of Government and the Private Sector in Implementing the PPP Scheme for the Cisumdawu Toll Road Project from an Infrastructure Sustainability Perspective

detail.title: The Role of Government and the Private Sector in Implementing the PPP Scheme for the Cisumdawu Toll Road Project from an Infrastructure Sustainability Perspective
detail.abstract: This study examines the roles of the government and the private sector in implementing the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) scheme for the Cileunyi-Sumedang-Dawuan (Cisumdawu) Toll Road Project. Using a document review and literature approach, the research explains how the division of tasks and risks between the government (as the Contracting Agency) and the Implementing Business Entity (BUP is organized, including the provision of feasibility support (VGF), land acquisition by the government, and the responsibility for financing, construction, and operation by the private sector (PT Citra Karya Jabar Tol/CKJT). The findings indicate that the hybrid financing model successfully accelerated the completion of the project, which had previously been delayed. However, its implementation faced significant obstacles such as slow land acquisition, financing issues in several sections, and gaps in governance and accountability. Consequently, the effectiveness of PPPs depends not only on financial aspects but also on the quality of coordination, transparency, and risk management mechanisms between stakeholders. Recommendations include strengthening governance, accelerating and opening up the land acquisition process, and implementing stricter oversight mechanisms to maintain a balance between public interests and the viability of private investment.

title: Mortgaging the Future: Financialized Time Collateralization and the Struggle for Temporal Sovereignty in Digital Capitalism

detail.title: Mortgaging the Future: Financialized Time Collateralization and the Struggle for Temporal Sovereignty in Digital Capitalism
detail.abstract: John Maynard Keynes's celebrated prophecy-that technological progress would yield a 15hour workweek by 2030-has failed. By the mid-2020s, a structural paradox is entrenched: while median Labour productivity in advanced economies grew by over 120% from 1980 to 2023, aggregate working hours saw only a marginal decline. This article argues that this failure is not due to a technological shortfall but to a systematic reclamation of time savings by capital through a core mechanism: Financialized Time Collateralization (FTC). Moving beyond standard debt theory, we conceptualize FTC as a temporal governance technology that securitizes workers' future Labour time, transforming systemic debt into a long-term, preemptive enforcement of capital discipline. Grounded in a critical-theoretical synthesis and empirical evidence-including a new Decoupling Index (DI) showing the U.S. (DI ≈ 35.3) as a paradigmatic case of high-finance capture, and illustrative global cases from China's "invisible poor" to platform drivers in India-this analysis demonstrates how FTC is operationalized and intensified by digital infrastructures and articulated with survival pressures. The struggle for temporal sovereignty thus emerges as the defining political horizon against capital's total capture of human life, necessitating interventions that target the very architecture of FTC, such as algorithmic transparency and universal basic income.

title: Nudges, Boosts, and the Intention–Behavior Gap: Evidence from a Cluster RCT on Methane Reduction in Rice Farming
affiliations: Meiji University, , Sophia University and

detail.title: Nudges, Boosts, and the Intention–Behavior Gap: Evidence from a Cluster RCT on Methane Reduction in Rice Farming
detail.abstract: Drawing on the nudge and boost framework in behavioral public policy, this study examines how distinct behavioral interventions influence methane mitigation in professional agriculture. We conducted a large-scale cluster randomized controlled trial (cRCT) involving 408 farming communities and 2,525 farmers in Japan, embedded within an agri-environmental policy program, to test whether information-based interventions affect both the actual adoption of prolonged mid-season drainage (MSD), a low-cost water-management practice that reduces methane emissions, and stated intentions for future adoption. By analyzing behavioral and intentional outcomes, the study addresses the persistent intention–action gap in climate-oriented interventions. Results show that social-norm nudges generated context-dependent increases in MSD adoption during the intervention year, particularly among farmers engaged in community-based agriculture. Although effect sizes were modest, leveraging existing extension channels implies that even limited behavioral responses can yield meaningful emission reductions at minimal cost when scaled regionally. In contrast, boosts in the form of procedural guidance primarily strengthened farmers’ intentions to adopt methane-reducing practices in subsequent seasons, without immediate behavioral change. Repeated information provision produced incremental gains in stated intentions, suggesting reinforcement effects over time. The results provide evidence on how behavioral tools operate within a developed-country agricultural sector at scale. Nudges were more effective for short-term behavioral activation, whereas boosts facilitated forward-looking commitment. These findings highlight the complementary roles of nudges and boosts in climate policy design and underscore that modest behavioral effects can warrant policy attention when achieved through cost-effective and institutionally scalable interventions.

title: Deconstructing Dollar Dynamics: A State-Dependent, Non-Linear Integrated Equation

detail.title: Deconstructing Dollar Dynamics: A State-Dependent, Non-Linear Integrated Equation
detail.abstract:
Traditional macroeconomic models, such as Interest Rate Parity (IRP) or Purchasing Power Parity (PPP), often fail to capture the extreme convexity of the US Dollar Index (DXY) during systemic crises and structural breaks. This paper introduces a novel, six-layer analytical framework that redefines the DXY not merely as a currency relative price, but as a state-dependent functional of global liquidity and market reflexivity.

We propose a Non-Linear Integrated Equation that decomposes dollar valuation into hierarchical layers:

  1. The Mechanical Layer: Redefining effective demand ($D^*$) to include Eurodollar repayment pressure and effective supply ($S^*$) constrained by collateral availability, rather than simple M2 money supply.

  2. The Modulator Layers: Introducing Systemic Instability ($\sigma_{system}$) and Reflexive Acceleration ($\kappa_{system}$) variables that mathematically model the regime shift of the USD from a risk asset to a safe-haven asset during stress events.

  3. The Psycho-Technical Layer: A critical update incorporating Algorithmic Homogeneity ($H_{soc}$) and Immediacy ($I_{impulse}$), demonstrating how Generative AI and high-frequency trading create a "Behavioral Phase Lock," rendering the market hyper-brittle.

  4. The Structural Layer: Quantifying the long-term erosion of dollar dominance via geopolitical fragmentation ($T_{frag}$) and alternative infrastructure ($C_{alt}$).

This framework provides a rigorous mathematical tool for quant funds and macro-strategists to forecast DXY behaviors in an era of de-dollarization and algorithmic dominance, moving beyond the limitations of linear correlation models.

title: Should Bangladesh Pursue a Free Trade Agreement with Japan? A Gravity Model Analysis

detail.title: Should Bangladesh Pursue a Free Trade Agreement with Japan? A Gravity Model Analysis
