The paper synthesizes evidence from leading institutions-including the OECD, IMF, World Bank, McKinsey Global Institute, Stanford HAI, MIT CSAIL, and Bloomberg Economics-to examine how AI reshapes global value chains, energy systems, sovereign compute capacity, scientific discovery, and economic diversification, with a special focus on Middle Eastern economies navigating post-hydrocarbon transitions. detail.title: The Institutional Crypto Bet: Are Early Adopters Buying at the Wrong Time?
detail.abstract: This analysis examines whether institutional investors are allocating to Bitcoin ETFs just as their diversification benefits are diminishing. While early research found Bitcoin had near-zero correlation with traditional assets (approximately 0.04 with the S&P 500 from 2010-2013), recent data from 2024-2025 reveals a stark change: Bitcoin ETF correlations with equities have risen to approximately 0.39, nearly ten times higher, and reached 0.49 by late 2025. As major pensions and endowments begin cautious allocations, this evolving correlation structure raises important questions about Modern Portfolio Theory's application to cryptocurrency and whether institutions are entering at an inopportune time for diversification.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly growing and becoming an increasingly important part of many industries, but it also raises significant ethical and social concerns. This paper looks at how algorithmic bias, which can come from bad data, poor sampling, labeling mistakes, and old patterns in society, can make unfairness worse in AI systems. These problems are not random but show deeper social issues that affect fairness, trust, and accountability. The paper explains how a lack of openness and oversight makes it hard to find and fix bias. To solve these issues, researchers suggest using clear data practices, regular checks on algorithms, and strong legal and ethical rules. Building fairness into AI from the start is key to making it more trustworthy. In the end, the paper argues that responsible and transparent AI can help technology support fairness and honesty in society.

title: Impact of Organisational Justice on Employees' Burnout and Workplace Cynicism in DHL International Ltd in South-West, Nigeria

detail.title: Impact of Organisational Justice on Employees' Burnout and Workplace Cynicism in DHL International Ltd in South-West, Nigeria
detail.abstract: This study investigated how distributive, procedural and interactional justice are practiced in DHL International Ltd in SouthWest Nigeria and examined their combined and relative effects on employees' burnout and workplace cynicism. Using data from 212 employees selected through stratified sampling across six states, the study assessed burnout dimensions (emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and personal accomplishment) and cynicism components (cognitive, affective and behavioural) through standardised questionnaires. Descriptive and inferential analyses, including regression, correlation, t-tests and chisquare, showed that organisational justice strongly predicted burnout (R = .895) and workplace cynicism (R = .635). Higher justice perceptions were associated with reduced burnout and lower levels of cynicism, with procedural-interactional justice emerging most influential. The study concludes that fairness in organisational processes and interpersonal treatment plays a crucial role in reducing negative employee outcomes and enhancing organisational effectiveness. It recommends that organisations embed justice principles to minimise burnout and cynicism, and highlights the broader applicability of the findings for private-sector management practice.

detail.abstract:
Coordination failures are not inevitable; they are artifacts of time. By collapsing commitment and settlement into a single atomic moment, cooperation becomes structurally dominant.

This paper introduces Structural Mechanism Design (SMD), a framework that shifts the objective from incentive compatibility to execution atomicity. We argue that global inefficiencies, from the $1 trillion wasted in supply chains to the fragility of financial systems, are not behavioral flaws but structural defects of sequential execution. By removing the temporal lag between commitment and action, SMD transforms intractable sequential pathologies (Holdout, Free-Rider, Bank Runs) into simultaneous Assurance games.

Crucially, the mechanism we propose is not new. Humans have been coordinating conditionally for millennia, from tribal hunters pooling resources for expeditions, to medieval guilds funding communal tools, to friends organizing group purchases. What is new is the ability to scale this ancient logic to millions of strangers who will never meet.

We present the implementation of this framework via Threshold-Activated Conditional Coordination (TACC) and the Vector Liquidity Protocol (VLP). VLP utilizes a Materialized Aggregate State to achieve constant-time O(1) verification, making atomic coordination viable at macroeconomic scale (n > 100,000).

title: Per-Country Caps and the Concentration of Intergenerational Harm: A Microsimulation of Age-Out Dynamics in The United States Employment-Based Immigration System

detail.title: Per-Country Caps and the Concentration of Intergenerational Harm: A Microsimulation of Age-Out Dynamics in The United States Employment-Based Immigration System
detail.abstract: The U.S. employment-based (EB) immigration system operates under two binding statutory constraints: a fixed annual limit of 140,000 visas and a 7% per-country cap. Together, these rules generate backlogs exceeding 1.8 million applicants and produce wait times that vary by decades across nationalities. These extended delays carry acute implications for dependent children, who lose eligibility for derivative status at age 21. Although prior research has estimated the backlog's scale and documented its unequal distribution, it has not produced a unified, petitioner-level model capable of capturing the queue's temporal evolution, isolating the specific contribution of the per-country cap, and quantifying child age-out risk under alternative policy regimes. This study addresses these gaps by developing a discrete-event microsimulation of the EB immigration system that reconstructs the queue at the petitioner level. The model integrates EB visa petitions from FY2013-FY2024, assigns dependents using nationality-specific demographic profiles, and simulates visa allocations incorporating per-country ceilings, their statutory exceptions, inter-category spillovers, and familybased spillover provisions. Calibration to the June 2025 USCIS backlog yields close agreement with administrative data, reproducing the total backlog within 1.6% and the India EB-2/EB-3 queues within 0.8%. The model is then projected through FY2035 under two scenarios: the current capped system and an uncapped counterfactual that removes only the per-country limit. Across the projection period, age-outs rise from 3,721 under uncapped allocation to 62,764 under capped allocation, an increase of 59,043. In the capped scenario, Indian children account for 98.8% of all age-outs, compared to 36.1% in the uncapped scenario. The findings provide the first integrated estimate of how per-country limits dynamically magnify and concentrate intergenerational exclusion within the U.S. EB immigration system.

title: Temporal Metaphor as a Method for Exploring the Japanese Linguistic Worldview
affiliations: MGIMO (Moscow State University of International Relations)

detail.title: Temporal Metaphor as a Method for Exploring the Japanese Linguistic Worldview
detail.abstract:
Time is one of the fundamental categories of reality, as no sphere of human activity can be considered outside of time and space. Each language reflects both universal features and the specific cognitive mechanisms for the formation of temporal meanings. In particular, temporal metaphors serve as a source of information about the cognitive processes that influence the formation of a nationally specific worldview shaped by the development of a particular culture.

This paper focuses on the conceptualization of time within the spatial model in Japanese and the specifics of the formation of metaphorical meanings of time expressed by the lexemes 前　後　後ろ　先. Three axes of conceptualization of spatial representations into temporal ones are examined: forward-backward, up-down, and right-left.
The specifics of the metaphorization of time in terms of space demonstrate the complex interaction between linguistic factors and the pragmatic aspects of utterance.

title: The Boundaries of the Farm and the Death of Small Banks

detail.title: The Boundaries of the Farm and the Death of Small Banks
detail.abstract: Using a novel source of exogenous variation in borrowers' structure driven by subsidy-induced consolidation in the agricultural sector, I show that as farms consolidate, large banks capture a greater share of deposits because large borrowers demand large loans, creating a comparative advantage for large banks. In response, large banks expand their branch networks and small bank mergers become more common, creating more concentrated local credit markets. The resulting structure reduces competition and reduces local deposit rates. These findings reveal how consolidation in the real economy can drive structural change within the banking sector and affect credit pricing.

title: Fiscal Geometry as Representational Infrastructure for Transfer Pricing

detail.title: Fiscal Geometry as Representational Infrastructure for Transfer Pricing
detail.abstract:
This working paper extends Fiscal Geometry (FG) by clarifying the scope of its two-axis fiscal plane and demonstrating its relevance to transfer pricing governance. While prior discussions of FG have often been read through a personal or household lens, this paper formally expands the framework to include both personal and non-personal fiscal carriers, including corporations, multinational enterprise groups, and other organizational entities that sustain post-tax capacity over time.

The paper preserves FG’s original axes: the X-axis captures cross-jurisdictional fiscal shifts triggered by rule-based events, and the Y-axis captures the continuation and redistribution of post-tax capacity across time and organizational succession. By treating individuals and enterprises as structurally comparable fiscal carriers, the framework accommodates corporate continuity, functional allocation, and profit-bearing capacity without altering the underlying geometry.

Transfer pricing is introduced as a maximal-fit application environment for this expanded definition. Shaped by dense interaction among domestic law, OECD-aligned soft law, tax treaties, and administrative enforcement, transfer pricing exhibits persistent institutional tension that is difficult to stabilize through narrative description or computation alone. The paper positions FG as a pre-analytical representational layer that makes such configurations visible and comparable for decision-facing review without imposing normative conclusions or replacing arm’s-length analysis, economic modeling, or legal interpretation.

For practical decision contexts, the paper also notes a minimal, bounded screening signal (0–1 ITI) to support prioritization and institutional attention allocation, while treating geometric validation (including optional divergence measures such as IDI) as a possible extension when deeper structural rendering is warranted. The paper concludes by specifying boundary conditions for use and outlining FG’s role as a complementary interface for human and AI-assisted workflows in transfer pricing governance.

detail.abstract: No existing legal order-national, supranational, or private-can evolve at the speed of exponential technological change without sacrificing legitimacy, enforceability, or both. The Universal Digital Law Codex (UDLC) was therefore designed from inception as a constitutionally dynamic private legal framework that explicitly mandates continuous adaptation, annual AI-assisted review, and legal garbage collection. The Codex further requires a UDLC DAO as the vehicle for this evolution, yet deliberately leaves its governance mechanics unspecified to avoid premature centralization. This article resolves that constitutional gap by demonstrating the perfect structural isomorphism between the UDLC's mandates and a decentralized governance architecture comprising a Weighted Directed Acyclic Graph (WDAG) forum, tight-coupling Validation Pools, non-fungible reputation (REP) tokens, Work/Availability Smart Contracts, and native anti-ossification mechanisms. When fused, these components operationalize the UDLC DAO as the world's first genuinely living universal private legal order. A legal order that delivers real-time adaptivity, days rather than decades. It is a global expert meritocracy earned through objective contribution accuracy, fully transparent and algorithmically weighted precedent, endogenous resistance to ossification, and long-term economic sustainability through reputation-weighted treasury distributions. The resulting institution does not merely improve upon existing legal governance. It constitutes a new genus: a self-evolving, meritocratic, economically self-funding legal system capable of providing globally enforceable certainty at the pace of digital innovation.

detail.abstract: This article reconstructs and critically evaluates John Rawls's theory of justice as fairness, with particular emphasis on its institutional orientation and its attempt to reconcile liberty and equality within a single moral framework. By examining the original position, the veil of ignorance, and the two principles of justice, the article argues that Rawls offers a compelling account of justice grounded in fair terms of social cooperation rather than individual restraint or historical entitlement alone. Rawls's focus on the basic structure of society highlights the moral significance of background conditions in shaping opportunity and life prospects. At the same time, the article contends that Rawls's reliance on ideal theory and abstraction limits the theory's capacity to address societies marked by historical injustice and structural inequality. Rather than undermining justice as fairness, these limitations clarify its role as a normative benchmark for evaluating institutions rather than a comprehensive blueprint for social reform. The article concludes by emphasizing justice as an ongoing moral project requiring continual critique, institutional reflection, and philosophical engagement.
